text: In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea

footnotes.text: The Greek verb παραγίνεται is a historical present — literally "John the Baptist arrives" — a vivid storytelling device common in Greek narrative that pulls the reader into the scene. English narrative convention prefers the past tense, so it is rendered "came," which also reads more smoothly aloud. The sentence deliberately ends without full punctuation, because the participles "preaching" and "saying" (v. 2) belong to a single flowing clause; the quotation that follows is the content of the preaching. "Wilderness" is preferred to "desert," since the Greek ἔρημος denotes uninhabited, unfarmed scrubland used for grazing rather than sand dunes. The title ὁ βαπτιστής could equally be rendered "the Baptizer," which captures its original force as a description of what he did, but "the Baptist" is retained as the familiar name.

"In those days" (ἐν δὲ ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις) is a Semitic-flavored formula from the Greek Old Testament, marking a new era rather than a precise date; it leaves the roughly thirty-year gap after chapter 2 unmeasured. κηρύσσων comes from κῆρυξ, a herald who makes a public royal proclamation in the open air — not a teacher lecturing but an announcer of news. ἔρημος, the source of English "eremite/hermit," describes a place of solitude and sparse habitation.

The wilderness of Judea is the barren descent from the Judean hill country toward the Dead Sea and the lower Jordan valley — steep, dry, and thinly populated. Prophetic and renewal movements repeatedly gathered there, and the Qumran community lived in the same region, drawing on Isaiah's call to prepare a way in the wilderness. John is also attested outside the Gospels by the first-century historian Josephus, who describes him as a good man who urged the Jews to virtue and to baptism.

By placing John in the wilderness, the narrative evokes Israel's exodus and the prophetic hope of a new beginning that starts outside the settled land and outside the temple establishment. John appears as the last of the prophets in the old mold — one whose whole role is to announce another — and later in this Gospel he is identified with the promised return of Elijah. Interpreters differ over whether his message is best read as continuous with the prophetic call to national repentance or as a distinctly eschatological summons on the eve of judgment; the Gospel seems to hold both together.
This verse is read in many traditions during Advent, where John's appearance frames the season as a call to preparation before the celebration of Christ's coming.

text: and saying, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near."

footnotes.text: The verse continues the sentence begun in verse 1: the Greek has two linked participles, "preaching... and saying," so "and saying" is retained rather than starting a fresh sentence, which keeps the flow natural for reading aloud. "Repent" renders a plural present imperative addressed to a crowd; other renderings such as "turn back," "change your hearts," or "change your minds" bring out different sides of the word but lose its familiar compactness. "Has come near" translates a Greek perfect tense: the nearness is an accomplished fact with a lasting result. "Is at hand" or even "has arrived" are defensible alternatives; "has come near" was chosen because it keeps both the sense of arrival and the sense of imminence without settling the question. Quotation marks and the comma before the speech are supplied, since the original has no such punctuation.

The verb behind "repent" (metanoeō) is built from words meaning "after" and "mind," literally an afterthought or change of mind; in its biblical use it carries the weight of the Hebrew idea of turning around and coming back, a reorientation of the whole life, not merely regret. The imperative is present tense, suggesting a continuing stance rather than a single act. "Has come near" translates engizō, from a root meaning "near"; the perfect form leaves a deliberate tension between "has drawn close" and "is now here." The word for "heaven" is plural in Greek ("the heavens"), reflecting Hebrew and Aramaic usage where the word is regularly plural in form though singular in meaning.

"The kingdom of heaven" is this Gospel's characteristic phrase, used dozens of times where the other Gospels say "the kingdom of God." The two are equivalent: "heaven" functions as a reverent substitute for the divine name. It denotes God's reign or kingly rule breaking into history rather than a place one goes after death. The tension in "has come near" has fuelled long debate: some read it as purely future and imminent, others as already inaugurated in the ministry that follows, and many hold both together — the reign of God is genuinely present yet awaits its consummation. Notably, John's message here is word for word the message Jesus will preach later in this same chapter's sequence, binding the forerunner and the one he announces into a single proclamation. Repentance is presented not as a means of bringing the kingdom about but as the fitting response to its approach.

By the first century many Jews avoided pronouncing the divine name and used respectful substitutes such as "heaven," "the Name," or "the Most High"; the phrase "kingdom of heaven" fits naturally into this pious speech and suits a Gospel closely engaged with Jewish readers. Calls to repentance in view of God's imminent intervention were a familiar note in the prophetic tradition and in the ferment of Second Temple Judaism, where various groups awaited God's decisive act to restore Israel. Preaching in the wilderness carried its own charge, evoking the exodus generation and hopes of a renewed people.

A few witnesses lack the connecting "and" before "saying," giving simply "preaching in the wilderness of Judea, saying." The difference does not affect the meaning, and the better-attested reading with the conjunction is followed here. The wording of the proclamation itself is stable across the manuscript tradition.

This call has long been read in preparation for Christmas, when John the Baptist is traditionally heard in the weeks of Advent, and it also serves as a keynote for penitential seasons and for services of confession. The single sentence "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near" is short enough to function as an acclamation or refrain.

text: This is the one spoken of through the prophet Isaiah, who said: "A voice of one calling in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.'"

versions.text: This is the one spoken of through the prophet Isaiah: "A voice of one calling in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.'"
versions.explanation: The participle λέγοντος ("saying") is left untranslated. Adding "who said" renders the Greek fully and also gives the sentence a natural pause before the quotation, which helps oral delivery.

footnotes.text: The Greek has simply οὗτος … ἐστιν ὁ ῥηθείς, literally "this is the one having been spoken of." The passive participle has no stated speaker, which in Jewish idiom points to God as the one who spoke; the rendering "spoken of through the prophet Isaiah" preserves that sense, treating the prophet as the channel rather than the ultimate source. The added "who said" renders the loose Greek participle λέγοντος, which hangs somewhat freely and could also be attached to the voice of Scripture itself ("saying"). The nested quotation marks reflect an interpretive decision about punctuation: the words "in the wilderness" are taken with "one calling" rather than with "prepare," so the voice cries out in the wilderness. The Hebrew of the quoted passage can equally be read "A voice calls: In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD," and the balance of the Hebrew poetic lines slightly favors that division; the Greek word order followed here is the one that shaped the Gospel writers' use of the text. "Make his paths straight" keeps the imperative plural addressed to a group, as in the Greek.

βοῶντος is a participle of βοάω, to shout or cry aloud — not calm speech but the raised, carrying voice of a herald. τρίβοι ("paths") comes from τρίβω, "to rub, wear down," so the word pictures tracks worn smooth by repeated travel; "paths" or "tracks" fits better than "highways." The adjective εὐθείας stands first for emphasis and functions as a predicate: "straight — make his paths!" The preposition διά with the genitive of a person regularly marks intermediate agency in the New Testament formula for prophetic fulfillment, distinguishing the prophet as instrument from God as speaker.

Some manuscripts read ὑπό ("by") rather than διά ("through") before "Isaiah," and a few add the article before the prophet's name. The reading with διά is the better attested and matches this Gospel's standard fulfillment formula; the variant with ὑπό looks like a stylistic smoothing that makes the prophet the direct agent. The quotation itself follows the Greek version of Isaiah closely but stops short of its final line, "make straight the paths of our God," reading instead "make his paths straight" — a shortening found in all three Synoptic accounts.

In the prophetic original the "way" is prepared for the LORD, the God of Israel, returning with his exiled people. By applying the words to John, whose preparation leads directly to Jesus, the text places Jesus in the position occupied by the LORD in the prophecy — one of the earliest and most understated christological claims in the Gospel. The change from "the paths of our God" to "his paths" allows the pronoun to point to Jesus. The passage also frames John's whole ministry as preparation rather than arrival: the repentance he preaches clears the road, but the traveller is another.

Roads in the ancient Near East were genuinely made ready before a king or dignitary travelled: obstacles cleared, ruts filled, routes levelled. The image would have been immediately concrete to hearers. The wilderness of Judea, where John worked, was also charged with memory — the place of Israel's formation after the Exodus and, in the expectation of the time, the place where deliverance would begin again. The same verse from Isaiah was taken as a program by the community associated with the Dead Sea scrolls, who withdrew into the desert to "prepare the way," showing that John's use of it belonged to a live and recognizable current of Jewish hope.

This verse belongs to the classic Advent readings, where John's cry frames the season's call to preparation. The words "Prepare the way of the Lord" have long been used as an antiphon and responsory, and they also appear in the liturgies connected with baptism and with the commemoration of John the Baptist.

text: John himself wore clothing made of camel's hair with a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.

footnotes.text: The Greek reads literally "John himself had his clothing from camel's hair," using the verb 'to have' with a noun for garment; English idiom prefers "wore clothing made of camel's hair." The emphatic pronoun autos ("himself") shifts attention from the prophecy just quoted back to the man, and is kept here as "John himself" for the sake of that contrast. The word osphys means the loins or lower back; "waist" is the natural English equivalent for oral reading. The final clause is literally "and his food was locusts and wild honey" — a plain nominal sentence retained as such, since the flat, unadorned listing carries its own force when read aloud.

Endyma denotes an outer garment or cloak rather than underclothing. Trichon kamelou ("hairs of a camel") describes coarse woven cloth, not a camel skin with the hide attached. Zone dermatine is a "leather belt" or girdle, the same wording found in the Greek translation of the Elijah narrative. Akrides is the ordinary term for locusts or grasshoppers, and meli agrion means honey found in the wild rather than kept in hives.

The description deliberately echoes Elijah, who was "a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist" (2 Kings 1:8). Matthew's readers would hear the allusion at once, and it prepares for the later identification of John with the returning Elijah (Matthew 11:14; 17:12). The clothing is thus not merely biographical detail but a prophetic sign.

Camel-hair cloth was cheap, rough, and worn by the poor — a pointed contrast to the "soft clothing" of royal courts noted later (Matthew 11:8). Locusts were permitted food under the dietary law (Leviticus 11:22) and were widely eaten in the ancient Near East, dried, roasted, or salted; together with wild honey they represent food gathered directly from the desert without cultivation, trade, or dependence on settled society. Some ancient interpreters, uneasy with insects, suggested the word referred to a plant or a cake, but the plain sense is the insect.
The manuscripts differ only in word order in the last clause, some reading "his food was" and others "was his food." The sense is unaffected and no translation difference results.
This passage is read widely during Advent, where John's austere desert life serves as an image of repentance and preparation.

text: Then Jerusalem, all Judea, and the whole region around the Jordan went out to him,

footnotes.text: The Greek verb ἐξεπορεύετο is singular ('was going out'), agreeing grammatically with the nearest subject, 'Jerusalem'; English requires a plural verb once three subjects are joined, so the rendering reads 'went out.' The verb is also imperfect, suggesting a sustained movement — 'kept streaming out,' 'were going out' — but a simple past ('went out') keeps the line light enough for reading aloud, and the sense of a continuing procession is carried by the piling up of the three subjects. The place names stand by metonymy for the people who live there; some renderings make this explicit ('the people of Jerusalem and all Judea'), but the translation keeps the Greek figure, which has its own sweeping force. 'The whole region around the Jordan' renders ἡ περίχωρος τοῦ Ἰορδάνου, literally 'the surrounding country of the Jordan.' Note also that this verse and the next form one Greek sentence; the comma at the end signals that 'and they were baptized' continues the same thought.

Ἱεροσόλυμα is the Hellenized, neuter-plural form of the city's name, which Matthew prefers over the Semitic Ἰερουσαλήμ; the two forms are used interchangeably in the New Testament. πᾶσα, 'all,' is repeated twice and functions as popular hyperbole — an idiomatic way of saying 'everyone was going,' not a claim that no one stayed home. περίχωρος is built from περί ('around') and χώρα ('land, region'), hence 'the country round about'; it was a standard term for the territory adjacent to a landmark or city.

The lower Jordan valley near Jericho lay a day or two's walk from Jerusalem, a descent of roughly a thousand meters through dry hill country. That crowds made this journey shows how powerfully John's preaching struck the nation. First-century Judea knew other renewal movements and other water rites — ritual immersion pools stood throughout Jerusalem, and the Qumran community practiced repeated washings — but a once-for-all baptism administered by a prophet at the Jordan was something new. The Jordan itself carried memory: it was the river Israel crossed to enter the land under Joshua.

The direction of movement is significant: the people go out from Jerusalem and the temple into the wilderness, rather than up to the sanctuary. Renewal begins outside the established religious center, and the nation symbolically returns to the border of the promised land to enter it again by way of repentance. The comprehensive scope — the capital, the whole province, the whole river region — presents John's ministry as a summons to all Israel, preparing the way announced in verse 3.

The text of this verse is remarkably stable across the manuscript tradition; the variants that exist concern only minor matters of word order and the presence of the definite article, and none affect the meaning.

This passage belongs to the classic readings of Advent, where John's call to prepare the way frames the season of expectation before the celebration of Christ's coming. It also appears in observances connected with the baptism of the Lord.

text: and they were baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.

footnotes.text: The Greek verbs here are imperfect and present: literally "they were being baptized... confessing." The imperfect pictures a steady stream of people coming one after another over a period of time, not a single mass event. English "they were baptized by him" keeps that sense of ongoing activity while reading smoothly aloud; a more wooden rendering would be "they kept being baptized." The phrase reads literally "in the Jordan River"; the Greek places the proper name first ("in the Jordan, a river"), which English naturally reorders. "Confessing their sins" translates a present participle running alongside the main verb: the confessing accompanied the baptizing rather than preceding it as a separate step.

βαπτίζω means to dip, plunge, or immerse, and was used of dyeing cloth and of sinking ships before it became a technical religious term. The preposition ἐν with the river can mean "in" or "with/by means of," but with a body of water the local sense "in" is natural. ἐξομολογούμενοι is a compound of ὁμολογέω ("say the same thing, agree, acknowledge") with the prefix ἐξ-, which adds the note of speaking out openly; the word suggests an audible, public acknowledgment rather than a silent inward admission. The middle voice adds a sense of personal, voluntary confession.

Some manuscripts read simply "in the Jordan," without the added word "river." The fuller phrase, which the translation follows, matches the wording found in the parallel account in Mark and is supported by early and weighty witnesses; the shorter reading may reflect scribes trimming what seemed a redundant word for a river everyone knew. The sense is unaffected either way.

Ritual washing was familiar in first-century Judaism: stepped immersion pools (mikva'ot) have been found throughout the land, and the Qumran community practiced repeated purifying baths. What set John's practice apart was that it was a single, decisive immersion administered by another person — hence "baptized by him" — rather than a self-administered and repeated washing. The site matters as well: crossing the Jordan was how Israel first entered the promised land, so a movement of repentance gathered at that very river carried overtones of a nation starting over.

Confession and baptism belong together here: the washing enacts outwardly what the spoken acknowledgment of sin admits inwardly. John's baptism is elsewhere called a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, and interpreters differ on how it relates to later Christian baptism — some see it as preparatory and provisional, pointing forward to the one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (v. 11), others emphasize the continuity of repentance, cleansing, and new beginning. The verse also sets up the sharp contrast of the next verse, where those who come without such confession are challenged.

text: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?

versions.text: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?
versions.explanation: Standard English punctuation introduces direct speech after "said to them" with a comma rather than a colon; the rest of the rendering is accurate and reads well aloud.

footnotes.text: The Greek γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν literally means "offspring of vipers"; the rendering "You brood of vipers!" keeps the traditional wording, which reads well aloud and preserves the single explosive insult. "You snake-children" or "you viper's spawn" would be more literal but would break the rhythm of the line. The added "You" simply marks the phrase as direct address, since Greek uses the vocative case with no pronoun. In τίς ὑπέδειξεν ὑμῖν the verb means "show, point out, give a hint," and it is rendered "warned" because the sense is that someone tipped them off about danger; "who tipped you off" or "who showed you how" are possible alternatives. "The coming wrath" translates τῆς μελλούσης ὀργῆς, a participle expressing something on the point of arriving; "the wrath that is about to come" is fuller but heavier for reading aloud. The question mark is kept because the Greek is a real question, though its force is accusing rather than curious.

γέννημα is formed from the verb "to beget" and normally refers to what is produced or born — including crops and produce. The same root reappears in the next verse's "fruit" (καρπόν), so the insult and the demand belong to one image cluster: what a thing produces reveals what it is. ἔχιδνα denotes a poisonous snake, a viper, not simply any serpent. φυγεῖν ἀπό is the ordinary idiom for fleeing away from a danger, and μέλλουσα, the present participle of μέλλω, conveys imminence — the wrath is already on its way.

The Pharisees and Sadducees were rival groups: the Pharisees emphasized oral tradition, ritual purity and the resurrection, while the Sadducees were largely a priestly aristocracy centred on the temple who rejected the resurrection. Naming them together shows that John's warning cut across the whole religious establishment. Snakes fleeing before a field fire or the harvester's blade were a familiar sight, and the image of creatures scattering ahead of destruction suits the question about escape. Snakes were also symbols of deceit and of hostility to God, so the insult questions their ancestry as pointedly as it questions their motives.

The "coming wrath" is God's judgement, presented as certain and near. John does not deny that people may escape it; he denies that a ritual washing without changed conduct will accomplish anything. The sting of the question lies in its irony: they have grasped that danger is coming, yet they have come only for the water. Interpreters differ over whether the wrath in view is the final judgement, an impending historical catastrophe, or both together; either way the text makes repentance, not lineage or ceremony, the condition of deliverance, which prepares for the rejection of descent from Abraham as a safeguard in the verses that follow.

Some manuscripts read simply "to the baptism" without the pronoun "his," and a few witnesses have "his baptism" in a different word order or with variation in the possessive. The sense is unaffected, and the translation follows the reading with the pronoun, which specifies whose baptism is meant.

This passage belongs to the traditional Advent readings on the preaching of John the Baptist, where the call to repentance in view of the coming judgement prepares the congregation for the celebration of Christ's arrival.

text: Produce fruit, then, worthy of repentance,

versions.text: Produce fruit, then, that is worthy of repentance,
versions.explanation: The relative clause "that is worthy" adds unnecessary words and breaks the rhythm for oral reading; the tighter phrase keeps the adjectival force of ἄξιον directly on "fruit" and reads more smoothly aloud, while preserving the mid-sentence placement of "then" for οὖν.

footnotes.text: The Greek reads literally "Make therefore fruit worthy of the repentance." The verb (poiēsate) is an aorist imperative, calling for decisive, concrete action rather than a gradual process; "produce" is chosen over "bear" because the Greek verb is the ordinary word for making or doing, not the agricultural verb for bearing. The inferential particle oun is rendered "then" and placed after "fruit" to keep the sentence's spoken rhythm and to let "worthy of repentance" land as the weighted phrase at the end. "Fruit" is singular, as in the Greek, and functions collectively; some render it "fruits" or paraphrase as "deeds" or "a life that shows." The adjective axios with the genitive means "corresponding to, in keeping with," so "in keeping with repentance" is an equally defensible rendering. The verse ends with a comma because the sentence runs on into the next verse.

Metanoia literally denotes a change of mind or purpose (meta, "after/change," plus the root for thinking), but in this Jewish setting it carries the fuller sense of the Hebrew idea of turning back — a reorientation of the whole person, not merely regret. The fruit imagery continues the agricultural language that dominates John's preaching in this chapter: fruit, root, axe, threshing floor, winnowing fork, chaff. The definite article with "repentance" ("the repentance") points back to the repentance John has been proclaiming, giving the phrase the force of "the repentance I have been calling for."

John's demand assumes that inward turning must become visible: fruit is the evidence of repentance, not its cause or its substitute. Read alongside the following verse, the point is that descent from Abraham confers no immunity — covenant privilege without corresponding conduct is barren. Christian readers have long discussed how this sits with justification by faith; the traditional resolution is that the fruit demonstrates the reality of the repentance rather than earning God's favor. The image also anticipates Jesus' own teaching that a tree is known by its fruit.

Some manuscripts read the plural, "fruits worthy," harmonizing this line with the parallel account in the third Gospel, which has the plural. The singular is the better-attested reading here and is followed in this translation; the difference in meaning is slight, since the singular is collective.

Repentance in Second Temple Judaism was expected to show itself in restitution and changed behavior, not only in fasting and confession; John's words would have sounded familiar in substance while radical in their target, since he addressed them to the religiously respectable rather than to obvious outsiders. Immersion rites of purification were widely practiced, which sharpens John's insistence that the ritual meant nothing without a transformed life.

This passage belongs to the classic readings for the season of preparation before Christmas, where John's call for visible fruit functions as the church's summons to self-examination, and it is also frequently read at the beginning of penitential seasons.

text: and do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you, God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones.

footnotes.text: The Greek verb δόξητε (from δοκέω, 'to think, suppose, imagine') governs the infinitive λέγειν, literally 'do not think to say.' Rendered here as 'do not presume to say,' which conveys the note of unwarranted self-assurance the idiom carries; other defensible renderings are 'do not suppose that you can say' or 'do not begin to say.' The phrase ἐν ἑαυτοῖς is translated 'to yourselves' (inward self-talk); it can also be read as 'among yourselves,' i.e. in mutual reassurance. Πατέρα ἔχομεν τὸν Ἀβραάμ places 'father' first for emphasis and is a claim of privileged descent; the wording 'We have Abraham as our father' keeps that force in natural English rather than the wooden 'We have as father Abraham.' The connective γάρ ('for') is kept because the second sentence gives the reason the boast is worthless, and the direct address λέγω ὑμῖν is left as the crisp 'I tell you.' ἐγεῖραι, elsewhere used of raising the dead, is rendered 'raise up' to preserve that overtone; τέκνα τῷ Ἀβραάμ is a dative of advantage, 'children for Abraham.' The verse is split into two sentences for oral clarity, with quotation marks marking the imagined boast, which the Greek signals only by word order and context.

Behind the Greek there is very likely a Semitic pun: in Hebrew and Aramaic 'stones' (ʾabanim / ʾabnayya) and 'children/sons' (banim / benayya) differ by little more than a syllable, so 'from these stones God can raise up sons' would have rung as wordplay in the preacher's own tongue. The name Abraham itself is linked in Genesis to 'father of a multitude,' which sharpens the irony of a boast about fatherhood. δόξητε is aorist subjunctive with μή, a prohibition against even entertaining the thought, stronger than a simple 'do not say.'

Descent from Abraham was a foundational marker of identity and covenant standing, and confidence in ancestral merit is attested in Jewish literature of the period. The setting adds force: John is preaching by the Jordan, where stones lay in and along the riverbed, and where Joshua had set up twelve stones as a memorial of the tribes crossing over. Prophetic tradition already spoke of Abraham and Sarah as the 'rock' from which the people were hewn, and of God's power to make a barren couple into a nation.

The saying dismantles any notion that lineage, birth, or inherited privilege secures standing before God; election is God's free act, not a family entitlement, and it can be extended to those who seem as lifeless and unpromising as stones. Read alongside later apostolic teaching, this becomes the seedbed for the claim that the true children of Abraham are those who share his faith, and for the inclusion of the nations. It does not annul God's promises to Israel but relocates their basis in God's sovereign grace, which is why the demand for repentance and fruit (v. 8) cannot be evaded by appeal to ancestry.

The wording is nearly identical to the parallel account in the third Gospel, which suggests a shared source preserved with unusual verbal stability. Manuscript variation here is minor and does not affect the sense: some witnesses differ over the presence of the conjunction introducing the quoted words after 'I tell you,' and over the exact form of the reflexive phrase 'to yourselves.'

With the surrounding call of the Baptist, this passage is a traditional reading in the weeks of preparation before Christmas, where it functions as a summons to repentance rather than complacency, and it is often paired with prophetic texts about a shoot springing from the stump of Jesse.

text: The axe is already laid at the root of the trees, so every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

versions.text: The axe is already laid at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.
versions.explanation: Two small refinements: (1) the Greek verbs ἐκκόπτεται and βάλλεται are present tense, conveying vivid imminence ('is cut down and thrown'), which the future 'will be cut down' weakens; (2) οὖν is inferential ('so/therefore'), not simple coordination, so 'so' better carries the logic and also reads with a cleaner oral cadence. 'Bear good fruit' is a more idiomatic and rhythmic collocation than 'produce good fruit'.

footnotes.text: The Greek opens with 'already' (ἤδη) in first position for emphasis, and the translation keeps that stress at the head of the sentence: 'The axe is already laid...' The small connective particle after it (δέ, 'and/but') is left unrendered, since English prose flows better without it and the sense is carried by the preceding warning. The verb κεῖται literally means 'lies' or 'is placed'; 'is laid' preserves the picture of the axe already resting against the trunk, poised for the first stroke, rather than merely being carried to the orchard. The inferential particle οὖν is rendered 'so,' joining the two halves into a single spoken sentence for reading aloud. The final two verbs are present tense in Greek ('is cut down... is thrown'), and the present is kept rather than converted to a future: it is the timeless present of a settled rule, with the force of something about to happen at any moment.

ἀξίνη is the woodsman's felling axe, not a small hatchet. The preposition πρός with the accusative here means 'up against, right at' — the blade is touching the root, the point where a fatal cut is made, not merely trimming branches. The fruit is called καλόν ('fine, sound, good of its kind') rather than ἀγαθόν; the word describes fruit that is visibly good and fit for use. ἐκκόπτω is a compound meaning 'cut out, cut clean off' — total removal, not pruning. Note the sound-play of the two passive verbs in sequence, ἐκκόπτεται... βάλλεται, which gives the clause a hammering, sentence-like rhythm.

The connective after 'already' varies in the manuscripts: most witnesses read δέ, while some read καί ('and'), and a few omit the word altogether. The parallel saying in Luke's Gospel has καί, which likely influenced some copyists. The variation carries no difference in meaning, and none of the readings changes the translation.

In the villages of Judea and Galilee, fruit trees — olive, fig, date palm, pomegranate — were long-term capital, planted for generations and taxed accordingly. A tree that stopped bearing was not left standing out of sentiment: wood was scarce in the region, and a barren trunk was worth more as fuel than as shade. Felling was done at the root so nothing would sprout again. John's hearers would have recognized an ordinary scene from the orchard, which is precisely what gives the image its edge.

The saying presses the point made two verses earlier about producing fruit worthy of repentance: descent from Abraham guarantees nothing, and judgment is measured by what a life actually yields. The image is individual as well as corporate — 'every tree' — so the warning cannot be deflected onto the nation as a whole. The fire mentioned here anticipates the fire of the next verse, where the Coming One baptizes 'with the Holy Spirit and with fire'; interpreters differ over whether that fire is purifying, destructive, or deliberately both, and this verse weights the destructive side. The word 'already' gives the saying its eschatological urgency: the time for repentance is not open-ended.

This passage belongs to the preaching of John the Baptist traditionally read in the weeks of preparation before Christmas, and it also appears in services of penitence and self-examination. Its stark imagery has long shaped calls to repentance in preaching and in hymnody.

text: I baptize you with water for repentance, but the one coming after me is mightier than I, and I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.

footnotes.text: The Greek preposition ἐν can be rendered "in" or "with"; "with water" and "with the Holy Spirit" were chosen for parallel rhythm and because the phrase describes the means of baptizing rather than merely the location. "For repentance" renders εἰς μετάνοιαν, which marks purpose or goal — a baptism that belongs to, and aims at, a turning of the whole life. The words "I am not worthy" translate οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανός, literally "I am not sufficient" or "not competent"; alternatives include "not fit" or "not good enough." The strong contrast built by the Greek particles μέν ... δέ ("I on the one hand ... but he") is carried in English simply by "but." The sentence has been broken into two for oral reading, since one long Greek period would strain the voice.

ἰσχυρότερος is a comparative of ἰσχυρός, "strong, powerful," and echoes the language of a strong man overpowering another; "mightier" keeps that force. βαστάσαι means to lift up and carry, not merely to touch. Note that here the task is carrying sandals, whereas the parallel accounts elsewhere speak of untying the sandal strap — two ways of naming the same menial service. The repeated ὑμᾶς ("you," plural) keeps the crowd, not an individual, in view throughout.

In the ancient world handling a person's footwear was the work of a slave. Rabbinic tradition allowed a disciple to perform many humble services for his teacher, but carrying or loosing sandals was regarded as beneath even that relationship. John therefore places himself lower than the lowest attendant of the Coming One. Ritual washings with water were familiar in Judaism, but they were normally self-administered and repeated; John's once-for-all baptism, performed by another, was something new.

"With the Holy Spirit and with fire" has been read in two main ways: as a single gift in which fire images the purifying, refining work of the Spirit; or as a double prospect — Spirit for those who repent, fire of judgment for those who do not. The surrounding verses, with their axe, threshing floor and unquenchable fire, support a strong note of judgment, while the later outpouring of the Spirit shows fire as blessing as well. The verse also sets John's whole ministry in a preparatory light: water and repentance point beyond themselves to the one who is mightier.

Manuscripts differ slightly in the word order of "I baptize you" (ὑμᾶς βαπτίζω or βαπτίζω ὑμᾶς), a difference with no effect on the sense. A few witnesses lack the words "and with fire," probably through assimilation to a shorter form of the saying; the wording is nevertheless very widely attested and is retained here.

This verse belongs to the classic Advent readings about John the Baptist and is also frequently read at baptismal services, where the contrast between water and Spirit shapes the prayers over the font.

text: His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire."

versions.text: His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor, gathering his wheat into the barn and burning up the chaff with unquenchable fire."
versions.explanation: The Greek has three parallel future indicatives (διακαθαριεῖ, συνάξει, κατακαύσει), and the contrastive τὸ δὲ ἄχυρον sets the chaff against the wheat. Rendering the last two verbs as participles ('gathering... burning up') subordinates them and loses both the parallelism and the contrast. Three coordinated future verbs with 'but the chaff' also give a stronger cadence for oral reading, building to the final phrase.

footnotes.text: "Winnowing fork" renders πτύον, a wooden fork or shovel used to toss threshed grain into the air. "Fan" is an older rendering, but it suggests the wrong tool to modern ears. The verb διακαθαριεῖ is intensive — "clear thoroughly," "clean out completely" — and here "clear" is followed by its object "threshing floor" to keep the line moving. ἅλων means the threshing floor itself, though it can stand for the heap of grain lying on it; "threshing floor" preserves the picture of a place being swept clean. κατακαύσει is likewise intensive (κατά + καίω), hence "burn up" rather than simply "burn" — the point is complete consumption. The Greek fronts "the chaff" (τὸ δὲ ἄχυρον) before its verb for contrast, and the English keeps that order — "but the chaff he will burn up" — which also gives the sentence a strong closing cadence when read aloud. The closing quotation mark ends John's speech begun earlier in the chapter.

ἄσβεστος is formed from the negative α- plus σβέννυμι, "to quench, extinguish" — literally "unquenchable," and the source of the English word "asbestos." διακαθαριεῖ is an Attic-style future contract form of διακαθαρίζω; the prefix δια- carries the sense "through and through." σῖτος can mean grain generally, but in contrast with ἄχυρον (chaff, husks, and bits of straw) it denotes the edible kernel. ἀποθήκη is literally a "place for putting away" (ἀπό + τίθημι), hence storehouse, granary, or barn. Note the repeated αὐτοῦ — his fork, his floor, his wheat — stressing the ownership and authority of the coming one.

Threshing floors were flat, hard-packed open areas, usually on a hilltop or exposed ridge where the evening breeze could be used. After oxen or sledges broke the stalks, workers tossed the mixture upward with a fork; the wind carried off the light chaff while the heavier kernels fell back. The chaff was then swept up and burned, since it made cheap, fast-burning fuel that flared brightly and was gone. John's hearers would have seen this every harvest, and the image of grain gathered and chaff burned was a familiar picture of decisive sorting.

Some manuscripts read "into his barn," adding the possessive to match the preceding "his threshing floor" and "his wheat"; others read simply "the barn." The shorter reading is generally preferred, the longer being easily explained as assimilation to the surrounding pattern. The sense is unaffected either way.

The image completes the previous verse: the one who baptizes with Spirit and fire also comes as judge. Wheat and chaff are not two crops but one harvest sorted — the separation is made within the covenant people John is addressing. "Unquenchable fire" has been read as describing the endless duration of punishment, and also as describing a fire that cannot be put out until its work of destruction is finished; both readings have long histories. What the text emphasizes is not the mechanics of judgment but its thoroughness and its certainty: nothing is left half-sorted, and the outcome rests entirely in the hands of the coming one.

This passage belongs to the traditional Advent readings, where John the Baptist's preaching prepares for the coming of Christ, and it also appears in commemorations of John the Baptist. Read aloud in worship, the verse forms the closing note of John's proclamation before Jesus himself steps forward in the next verse.

text: Then Jesus came from Galilee to John at the Jordan, to be baptized by him.

versions.text: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.
versions.explanation: The rendering is accurate, but the chain of three successive "to" phrases ("to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized") stumbles when read aloud. Combining the place and person into one phrase preserves the sense of both prepositional phrases while giving a smoother rhythm for oral reading.

footnotes.text: The Greek verb παραγίνεται is a present-tense form ("arrives," "comes on the scene"), one of Matthew's vivid "historical presents" that make the narrative immediate. English narrative convention — and the rhythm of reading aloud — favors the past tense here, so it is rendered "came." The Greek word order is literally "from Galilee to the Jordan to John"; the translation joins the two goals as "to John at the Jordan" so that the sentence has a single natural landing point and does not stumble over two consecutive "to" phrases. The closing phrase τοῦ βαπτισθῆναι ὑπʼ αὐτοῦ is an articular infinitive expressing purpose: "in order to be baptized by him." "To be baptized by him" keeps that sense while preserving the short, weighted ending that suits oral reading; a fuller rendering could be "for the purpose of being baptized by him," but that is heavier than the Greek feels.

Τότε ("then") is a favorite connective of this Gospel, used far more often here than in the other Gospels; it marks a new scene rather than strict chronological sequence. παραγίνομαι is built from παρά ("alongside") + γίνομαι ("become, come to be"), hence "to come to be present, to show up" — a slightly more formal verb than the ordinary ἔρχομαι, often used of a public appearance (it is used of John himself in verse 1). The verb βαπτίζω means to dip, immerse, or plunge; the passive infinitive here makes Jesus the recipient of the action, with ὑπό marking John as the agent.

The scene raises the question the next verses address: why would Jesus submit to a baptism associated with repentance and confession of sins? Christian interpreters have answered in several ways: that Jesus identifies with the people he came to save, standing where sinners stand; that he consecrates the waters and inaugurates Christian baptism; that he publicly accepts his messianic vocation as the servant who is numbered with the transgressors; and that, as verse 15 says, he acts "to fulfill all righteousness." Notably, the initiative is entirely his — he travels the distance and presents himself — which the deliberate purpose clause underlines.

The journey from Galilee to the Jordan baptism sites was substantial — roughly 100 kilometers or more on foot down the Jordan valley, several days' travel — so this is a deliberate pilgrimage, not a casual encounter. John's activity is placed in the wilderness of Judea near the lower Jordan, a region rich in symbolism as the place where Israel had entered the promised land. Ritual washing was familiar in the Jewish world through immersion pools used for purification, but John's once-for-all baptism administered by another, tied to repentance in view of the coming kingdom, was distinctive.

The wording of this verse is unusually stable across the manuscript tradition. The only variations are minor and do not affect the sense: a few witnesses differ over the presence of the definite article before "John," a normal fluctuation with personal names in Greek.

This verse opens the Gospel reading for the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, celebrated in many traditions at the close of the Christmas–Epiphany season, and it is frequently read at baptismal liturgies as the pattern and warrant for Christian baptism.

text: But John tried to prevent him, saying, "I need to be baptized by you, and yet you come to me?"

footnotes.text: The verb rendered "tried to prevent" (diekōluen) is imperfect, which here carries a conative sense — an attempt begun but not completed. Renderings such as "would have prevented him" or "kept trying to stop him" capture the same nuance; a flat "prevented" would wrongly suggest John succeeded. The compound prefix dia- intensifies the simple verb, so the resistance is firm, not a polite gesture. In the second half, the Greek sets two pronouns in emphatic contrast ("I ... you ... and you ... to me"); the added "and yet" makes that astonishment audible when read aloud, since English cannot stress word order the way Greek can. The final clause is a question in form but an objection in force.

Both pronouns egō ("I") and sy ("you") are expressed, though Greek verb endings already indicate person — a deliberate emphasis that frames the sentence as a chiasm: I—you, you—me. The present tense erchē ("you come") is vivid, describing the action as unfolding before John's eyes. The idiom chreian echō ("I have need") is stronger than a mere preference; it states necessity.

Some manuscripts read simply "he" rather than naming John; a number of witnesses also omit the name, while others include it. The sense is unaffected, since the previous verse has just introduced John, and the fuller reading may reflect a scribal clarification for public reading.

John's protest raises the question that occupied the early church: why would the sinless one submit to a baptism of repentance? The exchange preserved here answers it in advance — Jesus is not confessing sin but identifying with the people he came to save and "fulfilling all righteousness." John's words also confess the relative ranks he has already announced: the one coming after him is mightier, and John is unworthy even to carry his sandals.

John's baptism at the Jordan was a public act of repentance in preparation for the coming judgment, drawing crowds from Judea and the surrounding region. Ritual washings were familiar in Jewish practice, but they were normally self-administered; John's role as the one who baptizes others gave him unusual authority, which is precisely what makes his reversal of roles here so striking to him.

text: But Jesus answered him, "Let it be so for now, for in this way it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." Then John consented.

versions.text: Jesus answered him, "Let it be so for now; it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way." Then John consented.
versions.explanation: The connective γάρ is dropped, weakening the logical link between the command and the reason. Placing "for in this way" at the head of the clause also reflects the Greek word order (οὕτως γὰρ πρέπον ἐστίν) and reads more naturally aloud than trailing "in this way" at the end. Restoring the opening "But" (δέ) keeps the dialogue rhythm with verse 14.

footnotes.text: The Greek opens with the participial idiom "answering, said to him," a Semitic-flavored redundancy common in the Gospels; English rhythm favors the simple "answered him." "Let it be so for now" renders ἄφες ἄρτι, literally just "permit — now," with no object expressed; the verb ἄφες means "allow, let go, leave it," so alternatives include "Let it be" or "Allow it for the present." The adverb ἄρτι marks this as a concession for the present moment, not a permanent arrangement. The final clause is literally "then he permits him," with no name given; since Greek keeps the same verb (ἀφίησιν) as Jesus' command, John is clearly the one who yields, so the subject is supplied as "John" and rendered "consented" to make the sense audible when read aloud.

The verb ἀφίημι frames the whole exchange: Jesus says ἄφες ("permit"), and the verse closes with ἀφίησιν ("he permits") — a deliberate echo that ties command and compliance together. That closing verb is a historic present, a vivid narrative device that puts the action before the reader's eyes; English narrative convention normally renders it as past. πρέπον ἐστίν is an impersonal construction meaning "it is proper, seemly, becoming" — the language of what fits a situation rather than what a rule demands. Note the plural "for us": both Jesus and John share this obligation.

Some witnesses read πρὸς αὐτόν ("to him") while others have the simple dative αὐτῷ; the meaning is unaffected. A few manuscripts omit the pronoun altogether, and some place the verb of speaking differently in the sentence. None of these variants alters the sense of the verse.

"Fulfill all righteousness" has been read in several ways. Some understand δικαιοσύνη as God's saving purpose or requirement, which Jesus embraces in solidarity with the people he came to save. Others take it as obedience to the whole will of God, so that Jesus submits to John's baptism not because he needs repentance but because it belongs to the path laid out for him. Still others emphasize that Jesus identifies with sinners here, standing where they stand. The verb "fulfill" is a keyword in this Gospel, used repeatedly of prophecy and of the Law being brought to completion, which suggests Jesus is placing his baptism inside the larger sweep of God's plan.

John's baptism was an immersion tied to repentance and the coming judgment, offered to Jews as well as Gentiles, which made it striking in its own setting. John's protest reflects the natural order of teacher and disciple: the greater does not submit to the lesser. Jesus' answer reverses that expectation without denying John's own recognition of rank, and John's yielding shows him accepting a role he did not seek.

This passage is read in many traditions at the feast marking the Baptism of the Lord, near the close of the Epiphany season, where it stands alongside the descent of the Spirit and the voice from heaven in the following verses.

text: As soon as Jesus was baptized, he came up out of the water. And behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.

versions.text: As soon as Jesus was baptized, he came up out of the water. And at that moment the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him.
versions.explanation: Two small refinements: (1) "at that moment" flattens the interjection ἰδού, which functions as a call to attention; "And behold" preserves that force and reads well aloud, while also avoiding near-repetition with "As soon as" at the start of the verse. (2) "coming to rest on him" adds the idea of resting, which is not in ἐρχόμενον ἐπʼ αὐτόν; "coming upon him" renders the participle without importing wording from another Gospel. Otherwise the rhythm and flow are good.

footnotes.text: The Greek opens with a participle, "having been baptized," followed by the adverb εὐθύς ("immediately"). Rendering this as "As soon as Jesus was baptized, he came up out of the water" preserves the tight sequence while giving the sentence a natural spoken cadence; a more wooden option would be "And Jesus, having been baptized, immediately went up from the water." The adverb is attached to the coming up out of the water, not to the baptism itself. The phrase ὡσεὶ περιστεράν is rendered "like a dove"; it may describe the manner of the descent (gently, as a dove descends) rather than a visible bird-shape, and the translation leaves both readings open. "And behold" retains the Greek ἰδού, a narrative attention-marker that signals a sudden, wondrous turn; some translations drop it or render it "suddenly," but keeping it preserves the solemn, oral quality of the storytelling.

ἀνέβη ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕδατος literally means "went up from the water," implying he had been standing in it. ἠνεῴχθησαν ("were opened") is a divine passive — God is the unnamed actor. The Greek πνεῦμα means both "spirit" and "breath/wind," an ambiguity that recalls the Spirit of God hovering over the waters in the creation account. Note the double participle καταβαῖνον … ἐρχόμενον, "descending … coming," which slows the sentence and lets the vision unfold; the translation keeps both verbs rather than collapsing them into one.

Manuscripts differ at several points. Some read "immediately came up" while others have simply "came up"; some add "to him" after "the heavens were opened." A number of witnesses read "the Spirit" with the article, others without, and a few say "the Spirit of God" while some early ones read simply "the Spirit." There is also variation in whether the dove is in the accusative (agreeing with the Spirit) or another case, which slightly shifts whether "like a dove" describes the Spirit's form or its manner of descent. None of these variants alters the substance of the scene.

This is one of the clearest trinitarian scenes in the Gospels: the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, and in the next verse the Father speaks. The opening of the heavens echoes the prophetic longing that God would tear open the heavens and come down, and marks the end of a long silence. Interpreters debate whether the Spirit's descent is an anointing that equips Jesus for his mission (as prophets and kings were anointed) or a public attestation of who he already is; Matthew's narrative, where Jesus is conceived by the Spirit, favors the latter, with the baptism serving as commissioning rather than empowerment newly given.

Baptism by immersion in the Jordan fits the practice of ritual washing widely attested in first-century Judaism, though John's baptism was a one-time act of repentance rather than a repeated purification. Doves were common in Jewish life as the offering of the poor and appear in Jewish tradition as an image of Israel and, in some readings, of the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation. The heavens "opening" is standard language in visionary literature of the period for the boundary between God's realm and the human world being breached.

This passage is read at the celebration of the Lord's baptism, which in many traditions closes the Christmas season and opens the ministry of Jesus. It is also widely used in baptismal liturgies, where the descent of the Spirit and the voice from heaven shape the prayers spoken over those being baptized.

text: And behold, a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

versions.text: And a voice from heaven said, "This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased."
versions.explanation: The interjection καὶ ἰδοὺ is left untranslated here, even though the same phrase was rendered "And behold" in the immediately preceding verse; restoring it keeps the parallel structure of the two heavenly signs and preserves the oral cadence. Also, "my beloved Son" renders ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός more directly and reads more smoothly aloud than the relative clause "whom I love," and "in whom I am well pleased" matches ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα while flowing better after the appositive.

footnotes.text: The Greek has no finite verb here: literally "and behold, a voice out of the heavens saying." English requires "said" to complete the sentence, and quotation marks to mark the words spoken; both are supplied for the sake of natural reading. The Greek plural "the heavens" (a Semitic idiom, since Hebrew and Aramaic normally use a plural form) is rendered by the English singular "heaven," which carries the same sense. "My beloved Son" translates a Greek phrase that could equally be laid out as "my Son, the Beloved," where "the Beloved" stands almost as a title; the smoother adjectival wording was chosen for oral flow. "In whom I am well pleased" renders an aorist verb of delight; alternatives include "with whom I am well pleased," "in whom I delight," and "on whom my favor rests."

The word rendered "beloved" (agapētos) is built on the same root as the verb agapaō, "to love." In the Greek Old Testament it regularly translates a Hebrew word meaning "only one, unique" — most famously of Isaac, Abraham's "beloved/only" son whom he was asked to offer up. So the word carries both warmth and exclusiveness: not merely "dear" but "one of a kind." The verb eudokēsa is an aorist, which in Greek can express a settled, timeless disposition rather than a past moment; hence the present-tense English "I am well pleased." Some hear in it an echo of a decision made in eternity: "in whom I have taken my delight."

The words weave together two strands of Scripture: the royal enthronement declaration "You are my Son" and the opening of the first Servant Song, "Behold my servant… my chosen, in whom my soul delights." Jesus is thus identified at once as the messianic King and as the suffering Servant. Note that in this Gospel the voice speaks in the third person — "This is" rather than "You are" — making the words a public declaration to witnesses as much as an address to Jesus. Read together with the previous verse, the scene shows Father, Son, and Spirit together, and has long been treated as a foundational text for Trinitarian doctrine. Against an adoptionist reading, the traditional interpretation holds that the voice announces what Jesus already is rather than conferring a new status upon him. The same words return at the Transfiguration, with "listen to him" added.

Some manuscripts, notably one important bilingual codex along with Old Latin and Syriac witnesses and several early Christian writers, read "You are my Son" here, matching the wording found in the parallel accounts. This is generally judged a harmonization to the more familiar second-person form, and the third-person reading "This is" is strongly supported by the earliest and most widespread witnesses. A few witnesses also vary between "out of the heavens" and "out of heaven."

In Jewish tradition of this period, with the age of the prophets believed to have ended, God's word was sometimes said to come through a heavenly voice — the rabbis called it the bat qol, "daughter of a voice." Such a voice was regarded as a lesser echo of prophecy. The Gospel scene deliberately outstrips that expectation: the heavens themselves are torn open, the Spirit descends visibly, and the voice speaks directly and unmistakably, signaling that the long silence has ended.

This verse is the climax of the Gospel reading for the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, which closes the Epiphany season in many traditions, and it belongs to the ancient cluster of Epiphany themes — the visit of the magi, the baptism, and the wedding at Cana — as three manifestations of Christ's identity. The words are also widely used in baptismal liturgies and in blessings of water, linking the believer's baptism to Christ's own.
